transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, it's... I mean, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten completely out of hand lately. I just can't seem to stop launching new projects. And I don't just mean a little hobby here and there, I mean full-scale, intense initiatives. 

Like at work—I manage information systems—so I've been drawing up these massive, comprehensive work plans for the next three quarters, completely overhauling our deployment protocols. And at the exact same time, I decided I needed to fast-track a bunch of new certifications, so I built this rigorous, down-to-the-minute study schedule. But it doesn't even stop when I leave the office. I get home, and I'm instantly tearing into the walls to upgrade our entire home network because the current bandwidth is just unacceptable for what I'm trying to do. And while I'm running all that cabling, I'm also messaging all these old contacts from college and my last two jobs, pitching them on these new ventures and ideas. 

It just... it gets so incredibly intense, you know? The momentum just builds and builds, and I just blow right past normal limits, completely losing track of everything else, until finally my wife has to physically intervene at home, or my director at work has to actually step in and tell me to stand down. They're the ones who said I needed to come in, because I just can't seem to hit the brakes on my own once I get going like this.
During these periods when you're launching all these projects and feel so intense, do you find that you need less sleep than usual?

Oh, absolutely. It’s not even that I’m trying to stay awake, it’s just that the need for it completely evaporates. Like, my brain just decides that sleep is this totally inefficient, optional waste of time when there’s so much on the docket. 

There have been these runs, these stretches of days where I sleep maybe three hours, tops. I’ll finally force myself to lie down around midnight because my wife is begging me to, but then—bam—my eyes snap open, wide awake, sharp as a tack right at 3 or 4 a.m. And the crazy part is, you'd think I'd be completely exhausted, right? Like a normal person running on three hours of sleep would be dragging, chugging coffee, barely functioning. But not me. I don't feel tired at all. Instead, I feel like I’ve been handed this incredible gift of bonus time. 

It’s just so quiet at that hour, you know? No one is emailing me, the house is still, and I have all these uninterrupted hours to just execute my plans. I’ll just lie there in the dark for maybe two seconds, feeling this electric hum in my chest, and then I’m up, pulling out my laptop, mapping out server migrations or crimping those CAT6 cables before the sun even thinks about coming up. It just feels like I have all the energy in the world and sleeping would just be throwing it away.
During these intense periods when you're launching projects and feeling so energized, do you feel like you have special abilities, talents, or powers that other people don’t?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because... I mean, I don't know if I'd call it a "power," like a superhero thing, but... yes. Absolutely yes. When I get into that zone, when the momentum is just carrying me, I get this overwhelming, crystal-clear conviction that I am operating on a level that nobody else is even close to. 

Like at work, right? We have these massive, sprawling legacy systems, and most people—even the senior engineers, the guys who have been there for fifteen years—they just look at one little piece of it. They stay in their lane. But when I'm in this state, it's like I can suddenly see the entire matrix. The whole architecture just maps itself out in my head, all the dependencies, all the vulnerabilities. And at my absolute worst—or best, depending on how you look at it—I honestly believe, down to my bones, that I am the *only* person who can see it clearly. 

I'll sit in these meetings, and people are arguing about some minor deployment issue, and I'm just sitting there thinking, "You people have no idea what's actually coming." I get so frustrated because I can see the catastrophic failure that's waiting for us three quarters down the line if we don't change everything immediately. And I just know—I *know*—that if everyone would just stop talking, step aside, and follow my plan to the letter, I could single-handedly save the entire company from a major, multi-million-dollar collapse. 

I'll start drafting these massive reorganization emails, telling the VP of Engineering exactly how he needs to restructure his entire department to align with my vision, because in that moment, I am absolutely certain that I'm the smartest guy in the room, the only one who actually understands the stakes. And it feels so real, so undeniably true, that I can't understand why they aren't just handing me the reins and saying, "Lead the way." It’s just... it’s this absolute certainty that I am the linchpin holding the whole operation together.
During these intense periods when you're full of energy and launching all these projects, did you feel unusually happy, excited, or overly confident—like you were on top of the world?

Oh, absolutely. "On top of the world" almost feels like an understatement. Some weeks I feel... I mean, the best word for it is electric. It’s like there is a literal current running through my veins, and I am just completely, utterly unstoppable. I’ll be pacing around my home office or walking the floor at work, and I’m just buzzing with this incredible, high-definition excitement. Everything is clicking, every idea is brilliant, and I just feel this immense, soaring high because I'm operating at maximum capacity. It's fantastic. It really is. 

But... the flip side of that, and this is where it gets really messy, is that because I’m moving at lightspeed, everyone else seems like they are moving through wet concrete. And if anything gets in my way, that happy, euphoric feeling instantly sours into this intense, burning frustration. 

Like, if there's even a tiny delay—a vendor takes ten minutes too long to reply to an email, or a server reboot hangs for an extra thirty seconds—I just lose my mind. And it’s especially bad at home. My wife will come in and ask a totally simple, innocent question, like, you know, "Hey, are you going to stop and eat?" or "Can we talk about the grocery list?" And I just snap. I mean, I completely bite her head off. I get so incredibly angry because, in that state, it genuinely feels like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose. Like they are intentionally throwing up roadblocks to sabotage my momentum. I’ll start lecturing her about how she's breaking my concentration, how she doesn't grasp the magnitude of what I'm building... I just go from feeling like the king of the universe to feeling this explosive, skin-crawling rage, all because someone interrupted my train of thought for five seconds.
Can you describe how long these intense periods usually last? Like, from the time you start feeling this way until you come back down to a normal level of energy and focus?

Well, it's... it's not like a quick weekend thing, if that's what you mean. It's not just a couple of good days where I drink too much espresso and get a lot done. It’s... well, to really give you the full picture, I have to go back to when I first noticed it really locking in, which was, gosh, about a year and eight months ago. 

I remember the timeline specifically because it was right around the time we were migrating our entire backend database to a new cloud infrastructure, which was this massive, high-stakes project. And that’s when this whole... cycle, I guess you'd call it... really became a permanent fixture in my life. For the last year and eight months, these stretches—where I'm just incredibly driven, needing almost zero sleep, feeling like I can see the matrix and solve every problem in the company—they just take over. 

And as for how long a specific stretch lasts? It varies, but once that engine turns over and I get into that gear, I’m usually running hot for at least a week, sometimes two, sometimes even longer. It’s like a freight train, you know? It takes a lot of momentum to get going, but once it’s at top speed, it takes a massive amount of friction to slow it down. I’ll just be burning the candle at both ends, completely consumed by the work, the ideas, the absolute certainty that I have to get it all out of my head and into reality right that second. And then, eventually, it’s like the fuel line just gets cut. The crash is... well, it's abrupt. But yeah, this whole pattern, this intense, high-octane way of operating, it's been the story of my life for roughly a year and eight months now. It's just how I function.
After these intense, high-energy periods, have you ever experienced a time when you felt extremely down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for a period of at least several days?

Yeah, that’s exactly what happens when the fuel line gets cut, like I was saying. It’s not just a gradual winding down where I catch up on some sleep and go back to a normal baseline. It’s a total, devastating drop-off. I’ll go from feeling like I hold the entire company’s infrastructure in my brain to... well, there are these long stretches where I wake up feeling like a completely failed version of myself. 

It’s this profound heaviness, you know? Just heavy and flat. I'll lie there in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking about all those massive reorganization emails I sent to the VP, and instead of feeling proud, I just feel this crushing sense of worthlessness. The color just drains out of the world for days on end, sometimes weeks. I have absolutely zero interest in any of the projects I was just obsessing over. The mere thought of logging into my computer or looking at a server architecture diagram just makes me feel exhausted.

And it really bleeds into everything at home, too. During those high periods, I told you how I snap at my wife because I feel like she’s interrupting my momentum, right? Well, during these down periods, it’s the exact opposite problem. She’ll come in and ask completely normal, everyday questions—like, "Do you want coffee?" or "Did you check the mail?"—and even just answering her, just formulating a response and opening my mouth to speak, feels like too much. It genuinely feels like climbing a mountain just to say "yes" or "no." I just have no drive, no spark left whatsoever. It’s like all that electricity I mentioned just completely drains out of me and leaves behind this hollow, useless shell. It's so incredibly jarring because I know what I was just capable of a few days prior, and then suddenly I can't even manage a simple, basic conversation in my own kitchen without feeling completely overwhelmed by how empty I am.

inference_history.note: The patient describes a period of abnormally elevated energy, decreased need for sleep without fatigue, and increased goal-directed activity across multiple domains (work, home, social), with impaired judgment and need for external intervention. These features are highly suggestive of a manic episode, which points toward bipolar disorder. The current presentation does not provide enough information to specify the exact subtype (e.g., whether it's a first or recurrent episode, or presence of psychotic features), so a broader set of manic episode codes under bipolar disorder is considered.

The patient described intense periods of elevated energy, decreased need for sleep, and grandiose beliefs about their abilities, which supports the presence of manic or hypomanic episodes. However, the content does not yet clarify whether these episodes meet criteria for bipolar I, II, or cyclothymia. The previous candidates remain under consideration.

The patient's symptoms have persisted for over a year and eight months, with clear cycling between hypomanic and depressive periods. The duration and pattern of symptoms rule out Bipolar I Disorder, Current Episode Hypomanic (F31.13), as the patient describes more prolonged and recurrent episodes consistent with Bipolar II Disorder, Current Episode Hypomanic (F31.23) or Bipolar II Disorder, Current Episode Depressed (F31.33).
